abstract:
Groundwater is the main source of drinking water in Jharkhand, and the Singhbhum region in the south-east of the state holds India’s main uranium deposits. In-situ recovery (ISR) is a way of mining uranium in which a chemical solution is pumped into the ore underground and pumped back out with the dissolved uranium. If some of this solution escapes, it can pollute the surrounding groundwater, and such leaks are found only later, by manual sampling. No ISR mine operates in Jharkhand. This project is therefore a preparedness study: if ISR solution entered an aquifer in Jharkhand, how far and how fast would it spread, could it reach the shallow drinking-water layer, who should be informed, and what should be monitored?

To answer this, a web-based decision-support system named **JalDrishti** was developed. Its core is a groundwater contamination model based on standard analytical transport equations (Domenico and Ogata–Banks), adapted for fractured hard rock and fed with real Jharkhand data (CGWB water quality and water levels, aquifer maps, NAQUIM reports, GSI lineaments, IAEA deposit data) and ISR records from Texas, USA. In the uranium belt the rock permeability comes from the belt’s own pumping tests, checked against the mines’ dewatering records, and each run also gives a labelled hypothetical answer for rock permeable enough for ISR. An XGBoost model trained on 18,000 scenarios from the physics model gives fast answers with calibrated 80% uncertainty bands. The system also checks 397 government wells against IS 10500:2012, sends tiered email alerts to residents, ranks all 264 blocks by monitoring gaps, and runs online with five user roles.

The ML model reproduces the physics model with an R² (log scale) of 0.89 to 0.97 and keeps its 80% coverage on real-location tests; for the travel distance of radium it misses its target, which is reported openly. In the measured data, uranium is within its limit at all 342 tested wells, but nitrate exceeds its limit at 22 wells and fluoride at 32, and iron, arsenic and manganese have never been tested. At the hypothetical Jaduguda site the measured rock is too tight for ISR: in 20 years dissolved salts (TDS) spread about 30 m beyond the wellfield and uranium 4 m, against about 535 m for TDS in ISR-grade rock. In both cases the chemical indicators travel ahead of uranium. The 25 most poorly monitored blocks all lie in the uranium belt. Since no real ISR plume exists in Jharkhand, all modelled results are screening estimates, not forecasts.
keywords: Groundwater contamination; In-situ recovery (ISR) uranium mining; Contaminant transport model; Machine learning; Conformal prediction; Monitoring network; Decision-support system; Jharkhand; IS 10500.
